content.text:
**Выбираю кандидата 7**, уверенность умеренная. Я не прогонял все 30 дней по шагам. Сравнение построено на структуре планов и прикидке «издержки на день», так что второе место (кандидат 6) рядом.

**Как устроены планы.** Шесть кандидатов заказывают каждый день прогноз спроса, сдвинутый на срок поставки, умноженный на коэффициент:

| Кандидат | Товар 0 | Товар 1 |
|---|---|---|
| 5 | ×1,00 | ×1,00 |
| 0 | ×1,10 | ×1,10 |
| 6 | ×1,15 | ×1,15 |
| 2 | ×1,25 | ×1,25 |
| 1 | ×1,40 | ×1,40 |
| 7 | ×1,20 | ×1,00 |

Кандидаты 3 и 4 заказывают крупными партиями: 3 — раз в 3 дня, 4 — раз в 2 дня.

**Нехватка в начале у всех одинаковая.** Товар 0 до дня 3 и товар 1 до дня 5 живут только на стартовом запасе. Спрос по прогнозу — 71 против 39 ед. по товару 0 и 214 против 56 по товару 1. Эту неустойку не избегает ни один план, поэтому на сравнение она не влияет.

**Партии хуже ежедневных заказов.**
- У кандидата 3 фиксированные платежи меньше примерно на 27 в день. Но склад в среднем держит лишний дневной спрос, и хранение стоит около 32 × 0,6 + 48 × 0,9 ≈ 62 в день. В итоге примерно 76 в день против 41 у ежедневного плана.
- Кандидат 4: примерно 51 в день против 41.
- У обоих партии товара 1 длиннее при годности 4 дня, отсюда риск списаний. Кандидат 3 к тому же местами подходит к лимиту склада 252.

**Товар 0 стоит заказывать с запасом.** Недопоставка обходится в 11 за единицу (6 упущенной маржи + 5 неустойки). Излишек при годности 5 дней почти всегда переходит на следующие дни, и платится в основном хранение 0,6 в день. Поэтому выгоден заметный запас: ×1,2–1,25.

**Товар 1 запас не нужен.** Недопоставка стоит всего 5 за единицу (3 маржи + 2 неустойки). Излишек при годности 4 дня часто списывается, а это 10 закупки плюс 0,9 в день хранения. Выгоден заказ около среднего спроса, ×1,0–1,05 с учётом того, что множитель в среднем 1,046.

**Итог.** Кандидат 7 — единственный, у кого коэффициенты разные по товарам, и оба попадают в выгодные диапазоны. У кандидатов 5 и 0 мал запас по товару 0. У кандидатов 2 и 1 избыток по товару 1, а кандидат 1 к тому же может упереться в деньги в первые дни. Кандидат 6 (×1,15 по обоим) — ближайший соперник: немного недобирает по товару 0 и переплачивает за излишки товара 1.

**Выбор: кандидат 7**, уверенность умеренная. Расчёты приблизительные, в уме, без пошаговой симуляции по каждому кандидату.

**Как устроены планы.** Кандидат 5 повторяет прогноз со сдвигом на срок поставки: в день t он заказывает mu[t+3] товара 0 и mu[t+5] товара 1. Кандидаты 0, 6, 2 и 1 — тот же план, умноженный примерно на 1,1; 1,15; 1,25 и 1,4. Кандидат 7 смешанный: товар 0 — примерно ×1,2, товар 1 — ×1,0 (как у кандидата 5). Кандидаты 3 и 4 заказывают крупными партиями раз в 3 и раз в 2 дня.

**Старт одинаков для всех.** Товар 1 впервые приходит только в день 5: спрос дней 0–4 равен 214, а запаса всего 56. Товар 0 приходит в день 3: спрос дней 0–2 равен 71 при запасе 39. Эти нехватки неизбежны в любом плане, поэтому кандидатов они не различают.

**Редкие заказы (кандидаты 3 и 4) хуже.**
- Кандидат 3 экономит на фиксированной плате около 680 (примерно 2/3 из 25 × 41). Но запас в среднем держится на день спроса дольше. Это стоит примерно 18 в день по товару 0 и 40 в день по товару 1, около 1700 за 30 дней. Вдобавок товар 1 годен всего 4 дня, есть риск списаний и переполнения склада на 252 места.
- Кандидат 4 экономит около 500, а лишнее хранение стоит около 870.

**Ежедневные планы: какой нужен запас сверх прогноза.** Остатки переходят на следующий день и продаются первыми, поэтому лишняя единица стоит в основном хранения. Потеря на покупку бывает, только если единица успевает испортиться.

- **Товар 0:** нехватка обходится в 11 за единицу (упущенная маржа 6 плюс неустойка 5), хранение — всего 0,6, годность 5 дней. Значит, выгоден заметный запас.
  - Прибавка заказа на 0,1 прогноза стоит 1,2 на единицу прогноза.
  - Она окупается, если нехватка снижается больше чем на ~0,052 прогноза.
  - Переход от ×1,0 к ×1,1 явно выгоден, от ×1,1 к ×1,2 — примерно на грани, с лёгким перевесом в пользу ×1,2.
- **Товар 1:** нехватка стоит всего 5 (маржа 3 плюс неустойка 2), хранение — 0,9, годность 4 дня. Средний множитель спроса 1,046.
  - Переход от ×1,0 к ×1,1 стоит 1,0 на единицу прогноза в день.
  - Он даёт 15 за каждую единицу, на которую сокращается нехватка; ожидаемое снижение — около 0,05 прогноза, то есть около 0,75.
  - Это меньше затрат, плюс растут хранение и списания. Поэтому ×1,0 выглядит лучше.

**Сравнение.** Лучший расклад — товар 0 около ×1,2, товар 1 около ×1,0, и он есть только у кандидата 7. У кандидата 5 товара 0 мало, у кандидата 0 товара 1 слегка лишнего. Кандидаты 2, 6 и особенно 1 перезаказывают товар 1, а это даёт списания.

**Устойчивость.** Сделка асимметрична: у товара 0 нехватка стоит 11, а хранение только 0,6, поэтому запас по нему — дешёвая страховка от всплесков спроса. Товар 1 с коротким сроком годности при перезаказе быстро уходит в списания.

**Неопределённость.** Отрыв кандидата 7 от кандидатов 0 и 6 небольшой: оба сравнения (×1,1 против ×1,2 по товару 0 и ×1,0 против ×1,1 по товару 1) близки к равновесию.

I chose **candidate 0**. This is an estimate worked out by hand, not a full simulation, and candidates 0, 6 and 4 come out close to each other.

**How the plans are built.** Six of the plans (0, 1, 2, 5, 6, 7) order every day. Each one shifts the demand forecast by the delivery time and scales it by a fixed factor:

| Candidate | Product 0 | Product 1 |
|---|---|---|
| 5 | ×1.0 | ×1.0 |
| 0 | ×1.1 | ×1.1 |
| 6 | ×1.15 | ×1.15 |
| 7 | ×1.2 | ×1.0 |
| 2 | ×1.25 | ×1.25 |
| 1 | ×1.4 | ×1.4 |

Candidate 3 orders large batches every 3 days, and candidate 4 every 2 days.

**Where the daily plans lose money.** Orders are fixed in advance and leftover stock spoils. So any amount ordered above average demand (about 1.046 × forecast) is eventually written off at the full purchase price, plus storage. Ordering at or below the forecast leads to frequent shortages, because daily demand varies by about ±30%.
- **Product 0:** a missed sale costs 11 (6 lost margin plus a 5 penalty). The best level is somewhat above average demand, about ×1.1.
  - At ×1.2 (candidate 7), about 4–5 units a day spoil, roughly 55 a day.
  - At ×1.0 (candidate 5), about 4 units a day go short, roughly 44 a day.
- **Product 1:** a missed sale costs only 5 (3 margin plus a 2 penalty), while a spoiled unit costs 10. The best level is close to average demand, about ×1.0–1.1.
- **Candidates 1 and 2** over-order heavily, so they spoil a lot of both products.
- **Candidate 6** sits close to the best level but carries slightly more excess than candidate 0.

**The batch plans.**
- **Candidate 3** saves about 82 in order fees every 3 days. But the large batches add roughly 135 in storage cost over the same 3 days. Product 1 batches of up to 167 units also risk overflowing the 252-unit warehouse, for example around day 17. Within each 3-day cycle, a random demand swing can only be absorbed by the stock already on hand.
- **Candidate 4** saves 41 every 2 days, which is about the same as its extra storage cost of roughly 60. It ends up close to the good daily plans, with a little more risk.

**Result.** Candidate 0 balances shortages against spoilage best for both products. It is also the most robust when demand differs from the forecast, so it has the highest expected profit.

**Выбор: кандидат 7.** Уверенность умеренная: всё посчитано в уме по средним значениям, полной симуляции по дням не было. Отрыв 7 от кандидатов 0 и 5 зависит в основном от того, как работает перенос остатков между днями.

**Как устроены планы.** Кандидаты 0, 1, 2, 5, 6 и 7 заказывают каждый день по прогнозу, сдвинутому на срок поставки. Кандидат 5 повторяет прогноз один в один, остальные умножают его на свой коэффициент:

| Кандидат | Коэффициент, товар 0 | Коэффициент, товар 1 |
|---|---|---|
| 5 | 1,0 | 1,0 |
| 0 | 1,1 | 1,1 |
| 6 | 1,15 | 1,15 |
| 2 | 1,25 | 1,25 |
| 1 | 1,4 | 1,4 |
| 7 | 1,2 | 1,0 |

Кандидаты 3 и 4 заказывают партиями: кандидат 3 раз в 3 дня, кандидат 4 раз в 2 дня.

**Почему партии проигрывают.**
- **Кандидат 3.** Экономит примерно 27 в день на фиксированной плате 41 за заказ. Но склад между приходами держит в среднем лишний дневной спрос, и хранение обходится примерно в 62 в день (≈31 × 0,6 + ≈48 × 0,9). Вдобавок заказ товара 1 в день 18 (170 ед.) покрывает дни 23–25 с прогнозом 229. Это около 59 единиц нехватки и примерно 300 неустойки и потерянной маржи.
- **Кандидат 4.** Экономит около 20 в день, а лишнее хранение стоит примерно 31 в день. Тоже в минусе.

**Сколько заказывать сверх прогноза.** Средний фактический спрос примерно на 4,6 % выше прогноза.
- **Товар 0.** Единица нехватки стоит 11 (потерянная маржа 6 плюс неустойка 5). Единица излишка стоит до 12, но излишек живёт 5 дней и переходит на следующие дни, поэтому реальный убыток меньше. Значит, выгодно заказывать заметно выше среднего спроса, примерно ×1,15–1,2.
- **Товар 1.** Нехватка стоит всего 5 (маржа 3 плюс неустойка 2), а излишек — 10 плюс хранение 0,9 в день. Выгоднее держаться около прогноза, примерно ×1,0.

**Итог.** Кандидат 7 — единственный, у которого оба коэффициента попадают в эти диапазоны. Кандидат 5 недозаказывает товар 0, у кандидатов 0, 6, 2 и 1 избыток товара 1. Кандидатам 1 и 2 с большими коэффициентами, кроме того, в первые дни может не хватить денег, и заказы урежутся. Риск для кандидата 7 по случайности умеренный. Запас по товару 0 сглаживает всплески спроса. По товару 1 будут недостачи, но каждая стоит дёшево, всего 5 за единицу.

I estimate **Candidate 0** has the highest expected profit. I worked this out in my head without simulating every day, so the ranking is an estimate.

**What the plans are.** Candidates 0, 1, 2, 5, 6 and 7 all order every day. Each order is that day's forecast for the arrival date (L days ahead), multiplied by a fixed factor:

| Candidate | Product 0 factor | Product 1 factor |
|---|---|---|
| 5 | 1.0 | 1.0 |
| 0 | ~1.1 | ~1.05 |
| 6 | ~1.15 | ~1.1 |
| 7 | ~1.2 | 1.0 |
| 2 | ~1.25 | ~1.15 |
| 1 | ~1.4 | ~1.3 |

Candidates 3 and 4 order in batches instead: every 3 days and every 2 days.

**Batch plans (3 and 4).** These lose money on holding costs.
- Candidate 3 saves about 27 per day in order fees (41 × 2/3). But extra stock sits overnight: about a third of each batch on average, roughly 33 units of product 0 and 50 of product 1. That costs about 65 per day in holding.
- Candidate 4 saves about 20 per day in fees. Its extra holding is about 31 per day. The loss is smaller, but it is still a loss.
- Neither plan overflows the 252-unit warehouse.

**Daily plans.** The real average demand is about 1.046 × forecast, so the factor decides whether stock builds up or runs short:
- **Candidate 5 (factor 1.0)** orders less than average demand. Stock often hits zero, so it pays the penalty and loses sales on product 0. Each missing unit costs 11 there (6 lost margin plus 5 penalty).
- **Candidates 6, 7, 2 and 1** order more than demand. The surplus grows until it spoils, at 12 per unit of product 0 and 10 per unit of product 1, plus holding. For example, candidate 6 throws away about 3 units of product 0 a day, roughly 36 per day plus holding. Candidates 2 and 1 waste even more. Candidate 7 also over-orders product 0.
- **Candidate 0** is closest to the balance point. Its small surplus of about 5% over average demand absorbs random dips without large spoilage. On product 1, shortages are cheap (5 per unit) and spoilage is expensive, so 1.05 is a sensible level.

**Sensitivity to randomness.** Candidate 0 is also the most stable. Its small buffer covers days when demand is higher than forecast, but it does not pile up stock that spoils on low-demand days.

Candidate 6 is a close second. The difference between them depends on how much carried-over stock protects against shortages, and I judged that the extra spoilage outweighs it.

I pick **candidate 0**. This is a rough mental estimate, not an exact simulation.

**Which plans are which.** Candidates 0, 1, 2, 5, 6 and 7 all order every day. Each one orders the forecast for the day the goods will arrive (t+3 for product 0, t+5 for product 1), multiplied by a fixed factor:
- Candidate 5: ×1.0 for both products (exactly the forecast).
- Candidate 0: about ×1.1 for product 0 and ×1.05 for product 1.
- Candidate 6: about ×1.15 and ×1.1.
- Candidate 7: about ×1.2 for product 0 and ×1.0 for product 1.
- Candidate 2: about ×1.25 and ×1.15.
- Candidate 1: about ×1.4 and ×1.3.

Candidate 4 orders every 2 days, and candidate 3 every 3 days.

**Where plans lose money.**
- **Start of the month (same for everyone).** Product 1 starts with 56 units, but demand over days 0–4 is about 214. Product 0 starts with 39 units against about 71 over days 0–2. These shortage penalties happen in every plan and don't change the ranking.
- **Product 0.** A shortage costs 11 (6 lost margin + 5 penalty). A unit that expires costs 12, but leftovers keep for up to 5 days, so a small buffer is useful. Over-ordering builds up stock that eventually gets written off. At ×1.2 (candidates 7 and 2), about 4–5 units a day are wasted, roughly 50 a day. At ×1.4 (candidate 1) the waste is much larger. Around ×1.1 looks like the best balance.
- **Product 1.** A shortage costs only 5 (3 margin + 2 penalty), while an expired unit costs about 10 plus storage. That favours ordering about the expected demand, roughly ×1.0–1.05 of the forecast. Candidates 6, 2 and 1 over-order this product. Candidate 5 orders exactly the forecast, but the expected multiplier is 1.046, so it sits below expected demand on both products and runs short too often on product 0.
- **Batched plans.**
  - Candidate 4 saves about 14 × 41 ≈ 574 in daily order fees. But each batch keeps an extra day's demand in stock, costing about 18 + 42 = 60 in storage per cycle, which is more than the 41 saved. Net, it comes out about 250 worse than candidate 0, which uses the same factors.
  - Candidate 3 saves about 738 in fees. But holding stock for 3 days costs about 175 in storage per cycle, roughly 1,400 in total, so it is clearly worse.

**Robustness to random demand.** Candidate 0 keeps a moderate buffer on product 0, the product where shortages are expensive. It stays close to expected demand on product 1, where waste costs more than a shortage. That makes it the least exposed to both shortages and write-offs when actual demand moves away from the forecast.

**Ranking (approximate).** 0 is best, then 6, 4 and 7, then 5 and 2. Candidates 3 and 1 come last.

I pick **Candidate 0**, but with low confidence. Everything below is mental arithmetic and rough estimates; I didn't simulate any plan to the end.

**How the plans are built.** Candidates 0, 1, 2, 5, 6 and 7 order every day, and each order looks ahead by the lead time: the day‑t order roughly equals the forecast for day t+L, times a fixed multiplier. Estimated multipliers (product 0 / product 1):
- Candidate 5: 1.00 / 1.00
- Candidate 0: about 1.10 / 1.05
- Candidate 6: about 1.16 / 1.10
- Candidate 7: about 1.20 / 1.00
- Candidate 2: about 1.25 / 1.15
- Candidate 1: about 1.40 / 1.30

**Ruling out 3 and 4.** These order in large batches every 2–3 days. Product 1 keeps only 4 days, and batches of up to about 170 units of product 1 alongside product 0, against a 252‑unit warehouse, risk losing goods on arrival and having them spoil. They also miss sales between batches. I expect both to lose to the daily plans.

**Money.** I checked cash for Candidate 2 over days 0–5. It never goes below about 1,250, so no orders get cut. Candidate 1 orders more and may be tight early on, but that isn't what decides the ranking.

**Choosing the multiplier.** Average demand is about 1.046 × forecast.
- With fixed daily orders, extra supply above the average demand eventually spoils. For product 0 each spoiled unit costs 12; each unit of unmet demand costs 11 (6 lost margin plus a 5 penalty). The balance point is a little above average demand, around 1.1.
- For product 1, a spoiled unit costs 10, but unmet demand costs only 5 (3 margin plus a 2 penalty). That argues for ordering close to average demand, around 1.0–1.05.
- Candidate 0 fits both of these best. Candidates 6 and 5 are close behind. Candidates 2 and 1 should lose more to spoilage.

The gaps between Candidates 0, 5, 6 and 7 are small next to the day‑to‑day randomness, so the choice could flip.

I pick **Candidate 0**, but with moderate confidence. I estimated in my head and did not simulate each plan day by day, so this is a judgement from rough estimates.

**How the plans differ**
- **Daily-order plans (0, 1, 2, 5, 6, 7):** each orders the forecast for its arrival day (t+3 for product 0, t+5 for product 1), times a fixed factor.

  | Candidate | Product 0 | Product 1 |
  |---|---|---|
  | 5 | ×1.0 | ×1.0 |
  | 0 | ×1.1 | ×1.05 |
  | 6 | ×1.15 | ×1.1 |
  | 7 | ×1.2 | ×1.0 |
  | 2 | ×1.25 | ×1.15 |
  | 1 | ×1.4 | ×1.3 |

- **Batch plans:** 3 orders every third day (9 order days), and 4 orders every second day (13 order days).

**Why the batch plans lose**
- Plan 3 saves about 740 in order fees (369 instead of about 1,107). But its large batches, especially product 1 with its high storage cost of 0.9, add about 1,500–2,000 in storage. On peak days the warehouse also comes close to its 252-unit limit.
- Plan 4 saves about 570 in fees and adds about 900 in storage. Its two-day batches are also more exposed to random spikes in demand.

**Why the larger multipliers lose**
- Average demand is about 1.046 times the forecast. Unsold stock carries over to later days (until it expires), and shortages are lost sales. So day-to-day randomness on its own already leaves a running gap of roughly √T × σ units. Over the horizon that is about 37 units of product 0 and about 56 of product 1.
- Ordering above average demand steadily builds up surplus. That surplus costs the purchase price plus storage, and eventually it spoils. For product 0 at ×1.2–1.25 that is 100+ extra units at 12 each, much more than the shortages it prevents (11 per unit: lost margin 6 plus penalty 5).
- Product 1 has a thin margin: a missed sale costs 5 (3 + 2). An extra unit costs 10 plus 0.9 a day in storage, so a lean level close to average demand is best for it.

**Why Candidate 0**
- ×1.1 on product 0 adds about 40 extra units over the period, which is roughly the size of the expected shortage.
- ×1.05 on product 1 is about equal to average demand.
- Candidate 5 runs slightly short on both products. Candidates 6, 7, 2 and 1 overbuy one or both.

None of the plans can avoid the shortage of product 1 on days 1–4, because nothing ordered can arrive before day 5. This hits all candidates equally.

I recommend **Candidate 0**. I estimated this by reasoning, not by stepping through all 30 days, so the ranking is a judgement rather than a computed result.

1. **Plan structure.** Candidates 0, 1, 2, 5, 6 and 7 all order each day what the forecast says will be needed when that order arrives (day t + L). They differ only in how much they scale it up:

   | Candidate | Product 0 | Product 1 |
   |---|---|---|
   | 5 | 1.0× | 1.0× |
   | 7 | about 1.2× | 1.0× |
   | 0 | about 1.1× | about 1.1× |
   | 6 | about 1.15× | about 1.15× |
   | 2 | about 1.25× | about 1.25× |
   | 1 | about 1.4× | about 1.4× |

2. **Average demand.** Actual demand averages about 1.046× the forecast, so ordering exactly 1.0× falls short on average. That hurts Candidate 5 on both products and Candidate 7 on product 1. Each lost sale costs the margin plus the penalty: 6 + 5 = 11 for product 0 and 3 + 2 = 5 for product 1.

3. **Over-ordering.** Leftover stock carries to the next day and is sold oldest first, so any excess builds up. At about 1.15× and above, stock grows by roughly 4–9 units a day. It then exceeds the shelf life (5 days for product 0, 4 for product 1), so units spoil and their purchase price is lost. Holding costs and unsold stock at the end add to the loss. This hurts Candidates 2 and 1, and to a lesser degree 6.

4. **Batched plans.** Candidates 3 and 4 order in large batches every 3 days or every 2 days. These batches are close to or above the 252-unit warehouse limit, so units can be lost on arrival. Product 1 also spoils within the batch cycle, and these plans have more shortages between deliveries.

5. **Early days.** Every plan runs short in the first days: product 1 starts with only 56 units and receives nothing until day 5. This is the same for all candidates and does not change the ranking.

6. **Robustness.** With random demand, a small surplus of about 1.1× gives a buffer against high-demand days without large spoilage. That is why Candidate 0 comes out ahead.

I'd pick **candidate 0**. I estimated this in my head, not by running the full 30-day simulation, so it's a judgement call. Candidate 6 is a close second.

**How the plans are built.** Candidates 0, 1, 2, 5, 6 and 7 all order the forecast for the arrival day, shifted by the lead time and multiplied by a fixed factor. Candidate 5 orders exactly the forecast. The others scale it up:

| Candidate | Product 0 | Product 1 |
|---|---|---|
| 5 | 1.00 | 1.00 |
| 0 | ≈1.10 | ≈1.05 |
| 6 | ≈1.16 | ≈1.10 |
| 7 | ≈1.21 | 1.00 |
| 2 | ≈1.26 | ≈1.16 |
| 1 | ≈1.42 | ≈1.29 |

**Where the money goes.**
- **Start of the period:** the opening stock doesn't cover demand until the first orders arrive (day 3 for product 0, day 5 for product 1). That shortage happens in every plan and doesn't separate them.
- **Product 0:** a missed unit costs about 11 (lost margin 6 plus penalty 5). A unit left over at the end costs about 12 (purchase price plus storage). The two are roughly equal, so you want to order about the average demand, which is the forecast × 1.046, plus a little buffer. A factor of about 1.10 fits that best.
- **Product 1:** a missed unit costs only about 5 (margin 3 plus penalty 2), while a leftover unit costs 10 plus storage, and it spoils after 4 days. Ordering above average demand doesn't pay off here, so a factor of about 1.05 is right.
- **Ordering too much:** if every order is above average demand, the extra stock piles up for the whole month and ends as waste or leftovers that are worth nothing. That rules out candidates 1 and 2, and candidate 7 for product 0. Candidate 1 is also the only one where cash gets tight in the first few days.
- **Ordering too little:** candidate 5 orders below average demand (factor 1.00 against 1.046). Shortages build up steadily, worth roughly 450 or more over the period for product 0 alone.
